growth_story.headline: Spain's income per person rose in a credit-fuelled boom, shrank through a long bust, then climbed on reform, tourism and immigration to a new high in 2025.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2006 income per person grew 2.2 percent a year, a long boom that IMF staff later described as credit-fuelled and heavy on construction and housing. When the boom ended, growth turned negative: from 2007 to 2014 income per person shrank 0.9 percent a year, through a double-dip recession, heavy job losses and a banking crisis that closed or merged most savings banks. Wage moderation and the 2012 labour reform are credited with helping Spain create jobs and win back lost competitiveness, and from 2015 to 2025 income per person grew 1.7 percent a year, despite an 11.4 percent fall in 2020. Income per person only got back to its 2007 level in 2017, and in 2025 it reached its highest level to date. Recent growth has leaned on strong immigration and booming services exports, including tourism, while the sources describe productivity as lagging the European Union but improving.

threads.title: A credit-fuelled construction boom
threads.text: In the decade before the crisis, credit poured into building and housing. IMF staff found that construction, real estate and housing finance supplied over a third of growth in 2001–07, while wages and prices drifted out of line.

citations.title: Spain: 2012 Article IV Consultation (IMF Country Report No. 12/202)
citations.quote: Construction, real estate activities, and the housing-related part of financial intermediation contributed over a third of 2001–07 growth

citations.title: Spain: 2012 Article IV Consultation (IMF Country Report No. 12/202)
citations.quote: wage-price misalignments that have developed with a decade long, credit-fuelled, boom

threads.title: Bust, bank rescue and reform
threads.text: The bust brought a double-dip recession, mass unemployment and a shake-out of the savings banks, most of which were closed or merged. The 2012 labour reforms then helped hold down wages, and Spain began creating jobs again and won back lost competitiveness.

citations.title: Spain: 2012 Article IV Consultation (IMF Country Report No. 12/202)
citations.quote: The economy is in the midst of an unprecedented double-dip recession with unemployment already unacceptably high

citations.title: Spain: 2012 Article IV Consultation (IMF Country Report No. 12/202)
citations.quote: the number of former savings banks reduced to 8 (from 45 at the beginning of the crisis)

citations.title: Spain: 2016 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; Informational Annex; Staff Statement; and Statement by the Executive Director for Spain (IMF Country Report No. 17/23)
citations.quote: the 2012 labor market reforms have supported wage moderation and strong job creation, helping Spain reduce unemployment while regaining the external competitiveness

threads.title: Immigration swells the workforce
threads.text: Large inflows of migrants have expanded the workforce and made up for a shrinking native-born workforce. The IMF expects growth to ease as immigration slows and the population ages, and it says Spain is ageing faster than most of its peers.

citations.title: Spain: 2026 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Spain (IMF Country Report No. 26/102)
citations.quote: On the supply side, growth has been largely fueled by strong immigration, which has offset declines in the native workforce

citations.title: Spain: 2026 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Spain (IMF Country Report No. 26/102)
citations.quote: Growth should then gradually ease over the medium term as immigration slows and population aging intensifies

citations.title: Spain: 2026 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Spain (IMF Country Report No. 26/102)
citations.quote: the speed of demographic aging is one of the fastest among peers

threads.title: Tourism and services exports
threads.text: After the pandemic, world demand shifted towards services, and Spain gained more than most, in tourism and in business and computer services. The tourism boom began to cool in 2025.

citations.title: Spain: 2026 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Spain (IMF Country Report No. 26/102)
citations.quote: Spain benefitted disproportionately from the post-COVID-19 shift in global demand towards services, including tourism

citations.title: Spain: 2026 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Spain (IMF Country Report No. 26/102)
citations.quote: Spain’s attractiveness for higher-skilled non-tourism services—such as business and ICT services—improved on the back of past cost and non-cost competitiveness gains

citations.title: Spain: 2026 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Spain (IMF Country Report No. 26/102)
citations.quote: The tourism boom has started to normalize—real tourism services export growth fell from 12.4 percent in 2024 to 4.4 percent in 2025

threads.title: Productivity improving from low base
threads.text: Output per hour worked has risen since 2022, and the IMF finds productivity growth stronger than before the pandemic. Even so, the OECD notes a wide gap with the European Union, and small and medium-sized firms are much less productive than large ones.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Spain 2025
citations.quote: Spain has shown a positive performance in hourly labour productivity since 2022. However, it still maintains a significant gap with the European Union

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Spain 2025
citations.quote: SMEs, which represent 99% of all firms and employ most of the workforce, mainly in services, tend to be significantly less productive than large firms

citations.title: Spain: 2026 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Spain (IMF Country Report No. 26/102)
citations.quote: strong immigration has underpinned labor force gains, unemployment has further declined slightly, and productivity growth has been stronger than prior to COVID-19

since_last_year.text: Growth slowed in 2025, and the tourism boom began to cool. Income per person rose 1.8 percent, after 2.4 percent in 2024. In May 2026 the IMF still expected solid growth in 2026, despite the war in the Middle East.

citations.quote: Growth slowed from 3.5 percent in 2024 to 2.8 percent in 2025, still significantly outpacing the rest of the euro area

citations.title: Spain: 2026 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Spain (IMF Country Report No. 26/102)
citations.quote: The tourism boom has started to normalize—real tourism services export growth fell from 12.4 percent in 2024 to 4.4 percent in 2025

citations.quote: with solid growth expected this year despite the adverse impact from the war in the Middle East

growth_story.tension: The IMF describes a Spain that keeps outgrowing the rest of the euro area, but much of that growth comes from more people working, not more income per person. Income per person rose 1.3 percent in 2023, 2.4 in 2024 and 1.8 in 2025. The OECD says income per person grew more slowly than the economy because migration pushed up the population. (OECD Economic Surveys: Spain 2025, November 2025: "GDP per capita, however, has expanded at more moderate rates, largely as a result of a strong population growth driven by migration flows")
